name: Pantera Capital
title: RT by @PanteraCapital: Just wrapped Money20/20. My biggest takeaway as a VC: the two forces reshaping fintech right now are AI agents and stablecoins. @SirDigitalDan from @CoinflowLabs and I dug into both in our fireside. Some takeaways: * Where will value accrue? AI is collapsing the cost of cognition, and stablecoins the cost of settlement. This changes value accrual, when those inputs aren’t scarce. I’m expecting value to migrate to regulated trust, proprietary data, distribution, underlying physical assets, networks. * What does stablecoins as programmable money unlock? Funds and spending rules can execute together, letting a product enforce agent budgets or trigger conditional payouts with less coordination across banks, processors and operational teams. * Where is agent demand emerging? Dan pointed to compute, inference and data APIs, which agents need to complete tasks. I’m looking for infra on fraud, KYA, chargebacks, and merchant side ops to help proliferate agentic commerce usage. * Who carries agent liability? A purchase can comply with the spending rules and still be a mistake. Before delegating larger budgets, businesses will want audit trails, a way to dispute purchases and an agreement on who absorbs losses. * Where’s the distribution advantage? Local integrations and merchant relationships give providers access to existing payment volume. Stablecoins can improve settlement without changing how customers pay. (Coinflow connects cards, ACH and PIX this way.) * How do existing PSPs participate? A provider can earn a processing fee when a developer funds an agent by card, even if subsequent payments settle in stablecoins. (Coinflow powers card funding for Tempo’s MPP Credits.) Thanks for the week @money2020! Curious what others took away too!

name: Rob Greer
title: RT by @rob_svrn: Really interesting convo below from this weeks all in on why a16z stays away from the neoclouds, and it made something click for me about Bittensor. @bhorowitz point is that scaling compute on debt is a dangerous arbitrage business, and he lived it in 99 when bandwidth was $1,500/megabit and the only way to get it was a 3 year contract. By 2001 it was $50 - If you were holding that on borrowed money you were dead. His case for $CRWV being different is that AI compute is in a massive shortage, so GPU and data center prices keep rising. Maybe he's right. But the neocloud model is still a levered bet that GPU scarcity outlasts the debt, because they borrow against the GPUs and the lenders get paid on a schedule whether or not the market cooperates. A compute subnet on Bittensor is basically a decentralized neocloud that doesn't need any of that. There's no GPU purchase to finance (miners show up with their own hardware) and no 3 year capacity contract to get stuck holding if prices move. The token + the network do the job the debt does for CoreWeave. Emissions bootstrap the supply side, and as demand and revenue grow the subnet puts that value back into its token, which raises what miners earn and pulls more compute onto the network. The token is the lever that scales how much compute you can harvest and coordinate. So if GPU pricing ever pulls a Loudcloud, the subnet doesn't blow up, its incentives just buy more compute than they used to. With no debt there's nothing to default on, and nobody can call a loan or force a fire sale. The risk you take on instead is token volatility, which you manage with a treasury (keep cash on hand and use it to support your token through drawdowns). A bad market can starve a subnet for a while, but one with real demand underneath it can ride that out. The tradeoff is a slower, more gradual build. A neocloud can borrow its way to a giant cluster fast, while a subnet's capacity grows with the size of the network and the token. What you get in exchange is a far more durable business, mostly because of where the supply comes from. You're tapping a bunch of long tails of compute that a neocloud can't really get at: >people who own their own hardware and want to monetize it when they're not using it >slack capacity in data centers (nobody runs at 100%), which can get sold into the subnet's spot market instead of sitting idle >sunk cost hardware, i.e. paid off GPUs that can't get a contract for anything else >operators in places with cheap power that no lender would ever underwrite a data center for Once a card is paid off the main ongoing cost is power, which even on an H100 is something like 5-10 cents an hour depending on where you are. So a lot of this supply is pretty price insensitive. They make more when the token is higher, but a 50% drawdown in miner rewards eats into their margin and plenty of them keep mining anyway. That gives you a structural supply floor that doesn't really care what the token (and therefore the miner reward) is doing day to day. Then as network value and the token go up, you progressively unlock compute that's more price sensitive (financed GPUs that still have to pay themselves off, US data centers with pricier power, etc). Each one joins once mining becomes economic for it, and you get a flywheel: token up → more of the world's compute profitable to plug in → more capacity to sell → more revenue → more value back into the token → repeat. Every GPU that joins also makes the network cheaper and more reliable to buy from, so you get a real network effect on top of removing the debt risk. And in the limit it can reach more compute than any single hyperscaler could ever build or finance, because the supply side is permissionless and global. You start by tapping into the world's edge compute, and over time the rest of the world's compute comes online as it makes economic sense for whoever owns it.

title: In an AI compute short squeeze, everyone in the stack looks smart. That doesn’t tell you who earns durable long-term returns. You can be right on demand and still own the wrong businesses. Today we estimate that every incremental GW of data center capacity currently generates $40-50bn of revenue across the stack. Data centers are under-earning (~$2.2mn/MW) relative to the value they unlock at the token factory layer (~$40mn+/MW). Frontier models face real pricing pressure from open-source and the hyperscalers. A 40% token-price cut can push standalone inference near breakeven — while hyperscalers still make money on the hardware. The picture will look very different in 6–12 months. Energy capacity, tokens per watt, model-layer competition, and financing are all in motion. We built a dynamic tool to track how it plays out. This map will look different in 6-12 months. Four forces to watch: - Energy, the most acute bottleneck today - More tokens per watt from better hardware and software - Rising competition at the model layer - Financing all this capex So we open-sourced our model. Input your assumptions and watch how value shifts across the stack.

name: SemiAnalysis
title: Every data center leaves a trail before it’s built. We track all of it. “We published a deep dive in our industrials model on a company called Sterling. They do early-stage construction: the groundbreaking, the site work. That’s the first thing that happens when one of these projects starts getting built. We were able to predict their orders were going to surge, which is exactly what happened.” “There’s essentially this waterfall of things we can track. Electrical and cooling equipment comes after. Energy has very long lead times; everyone knows gas turbines are multiple years out. We look at all of that to ensure our timelines are accurate.” “Pre-leasing is even earlier. Hyperscalers, neoclouds and AI labs signing lease contracts with data center operators. It helps us understand ahead of time what’s going to get built under these binding contracts that cannot be canceled.”

title: The future of cybersecurity will be dictated by a defender's ability to not only ingest unique attacks, but generate the strains that don't exist yet and ship the detection ahead of them. As the rest of the industry degrades, the largest financial institutions will consolidate on the single provider that can do this at scale. That provider needs a constant supply of unique attacks to work from, and a subnet is the only structure that pays a swarm of attackers to supply them. bittensor:native #SN61
